title: Unending Cruelties Against Eelam Tamils!
translatorNote: This translation is intended to carry Kalaignar's voice into clear, contemporary English rather than recast the letter as literary or academic prose. It preserves the source's argument, political directness, rhetorical questions, repetition, irony, factual detail, and paragraph order. Names, dates, figures, quotations, and intentional English expressions are retained. Where Tamil idiom cannot be reproduced literally without sounding unnatural, the English follows its sense and rhetorical force without adding claims absent from the source. The original Tamil is reproduced in full below the translation and remains the authoritative text. `Udanpirappē` is retained in Tamil transliteration rather than flattened into “brother,” “sister,” or “comrade.” Literally evoking “one born alongside me,” Kalaignar uses it as a distinctive address of shared identity, equality, affection, and solidarity within the movement. Letter-specific notes: 1. Statements about land seizure, destruction of religious sites, military conduct and human-rights violations are translated as allegations, reports, resolutions or claims presented by the source; the English does not independently establish them as fact. 2. **Human Rights Watch**, **Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group**, **TESO**, **Palk Strait** and the cited ship names are rendered according to the source context and the existing Volume 48 glossary/style lock. 3. The letter deliberately resumes the Dubai-refugee issue discussed in 3741 and records the author's report that the 19 people would not be returned to Sri Lanka; this is preserved as the source's stated development.
paragraphs: Forty-five Eelam Tamils who tried to cross the sea to escape the Sri Lankan military and save themselves were caught. On 23 April 2013, I had appealed that the Government of India take immediate action to relieve their distress, after reports reached us that of those put ashore in Dubai, the U.N. had ordered 19 to be sent back to Sri Lanka; Sweden had accepted eight; the United States had promised asylum to 11; seven had already been sent back to Colombo; no country had come forward to give asylum to the remaining 19; and the Dubai government was preparing to send them back to Colombo.

Union Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, after reading this appeal of mine published in Murasoli on the 23rd, sent word that the Union Government had considered it and that those 19 Eelam Tamils in Dubai would not be sent back to Sri Lanka. I have also received information to that effect from the Eelam Tamils who were being held in Dubai. On behalf of Eelam Tamils, I convey my thanks to the Union Government and to the Finance Minister for this. Even so, I am duty-bound to point out that the Government of India remains slow in acting to remove the continuing hardships inflicted upon Eelam Tamils in Sri Lanka.

Further, on the 22nd, when India's Defence Minister Antony answered a question in the Lok Sabha about the frequent attacks on Tamil Nadu fishermen by the Sri Lankan Navy, he said that India had advised the Sri Lankan government to instruct the Sri Lankan military not to attack fishermen who come near the international maritime boundary and to act humanely, and that India would continue taking steps to safeguard the welfare of Indian fishermen.

He further told the Lok Sabha: “An agreement was reached between the two countries on this issue in October 2008. Under it, the Sri Lankan Navy must not fire on Indian fishing boats. Indian naval vessels and Coast Guard vessels have been stationed in the Palk Strait region to prevent illegal activities in Indian waters and to prevent attacks on Indian fishermen fishing in our waters.”

Yet the Sinhala government, which respects no agreement, has not respected this agreement either. The cruel incidents in which Tamil Nadu fishermen have continued to be attacked even after 2008 keep proving this.

It is with all this in mind that we in TESO have been saying that the Commonwealth conference must not be held in Sri Lanka. In the statement I issued on 23 April 2013, I referred to the Commonwealth Law Conference held in Cape Town, South Africa, from 14 April to 18 April and to the participation of 27 Chief Justices from Commonwealth countries. I pointed out that in a resolution adopted unanimously they called for the Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group meeting in London on 26 April 2013 to consider the Sri Lankan issue and decide whether Sri Lanka should be removed from the Commonwealth; said that removal had assumed importance because of continuing human-rights violations in Sri Lanka and violations of the Commonwealth's fundamental principles; and called for reconsideration of holding the Commonwealth conference in Sri Lanka.

Following this, while we have urged the Government of India, DMK Members of Parliament have also been meeting ambassadors of Commonwealth countries and making the same appeal. Adding further strength to our demand, Brad Adams, Asia Director of Human Rights Watch, has urged:

“Sri Lanka's Chief Justice has been removed; the press is being suppressed; fundamental freedoms are denied and human-rights violations continue. If a Commonwealth conference is held in such a country, it will amount to approval of the Sri Lankan government's human-rights violations. Until the Sri Lankan government takes proper action on human rights, the Commonwealth conference must not be held there. This must be discussed at the meeting in London and Sri Lanka must be warned. Member countries must place on record that a Commonwealth conference cannot be held in a country that does not respect human rights.”

As another example of the extent to which, according to the source, the Sri Lankan government's human-rights violations have gone beyond limits, 6,381 acres of land belonging to Tamils in Sri Lanka have been illegally occupied by the Sinhala military. This occupation has continued since the Valikamam area of Jaffna came under Sinhala military control in 1990. After the war ended, there had been an expectation that these lands would be returned to Tamils. Instead, the source says, the Sinhala government has now issued an order to make these lands the property of the Sinhala military itself.

Such occupation is said to be taking place intensively not only in the Jaffna region but also in the Tamil-owned areas of Kilinochchi, Mullaitivu, Vavuniya, Mannar, Trincomalee, Batticaloa and Ampara districts.

It is further reported that the Sri Lankan government plans to construct the military headquarters for the Jaffna region on this Tamil-owned land. About 2,500 temples at which Tamils worshipped and 400 Christian churches are said to have been demolished and Sinhala places of worship established there. Information to this effect has been sent from there, and Tamils are said to be engaging in peaceful protest against it.
These demands of Eelam Tamils were already addressed in resolutions adopted at the grand TESO conference held in Chennai on 12 August 2012. One resolution said:

“In present-day Sri Lanka, military domination has overtaken democratic government. For its activities, the military has taken over a large number of houses belonging to Tamils in Tamil areas. The military takes control of vacant houses and refuses to vacate them. Without military permission, no social function can be held in Tamil homes in the Northern and Eastern regions. Military personnel themselves are appointed there as District Collectors and government administrators. Today's Tamil Eelam looks like a military camp. Because democratic local-government bodies do not exist, Tamils there have no way to voice their grievances, speak, or protest peacefully. They remain frozen in great fear at all times. This conference therefore calls upon the United Nations and the countries of the world to pressure the Sri Lankan government to withdraw the military immediately from Tamil Eelam areas. The United Nations should establish an international body to directly monitor the military withdrawal.”

“Sinhala fishermen are being settled in the Northern and Eastern coastal areas where Tamil fishermen have lived for generations. As a result, the livelihood of Tamil fishermen has been affected. The Sinhala people forcibly settled in these areas must be sent back immediately, and Tamils must once again be recognised as having rights over the sources of their occupations, commerce and natural resources. The U.N. must press the Sri Lankan government to undertake immediately the work necessary to restore normal life for Tamils.”

In order to defeat these efforts by the Sinhala military to occupy and seize the lands in Sri Lanka where Tamils lived and which belonged to them, I once again urge that our Government of India in particular, along with the countries of the world and the United Nations, intervene immediately; recover these lands that rightfully belong to Eelam Tamils; take appropriate action so that they may continue to live there; and ensure that the Sinhala military leaves the areas in which Tamils lived.
